about: THE WENDS AND THE BALTIC SHORE, 780-1070 - the Obodrites, the Wilzi (from the 980s the Lutici), the Pomeranians, the Prussians (Wulfstan's Este) and the Curonians: who rules in any year, the wars, the raids on trading places, the laws and customs a merchant meets, the money, the church. Research for the game's writers, 4 Oct 2026. Every entry names its source by work and chapter or year entry; the wording is our own and nothing is quoted from a modern translation. (?) marks what is uncertain, or was written from memory and not checked again tonight: chapter numbers of Widukind, Thietmar, Adam and the charters should be checked against an edition before any is shown to a player. Years are AD, Julian. In 'rulers', 'realm' is the people (obodrites, prussians and curonians are realm ids in ports_793.json; wilzi and pomeranians have no port in that table yet); from/to are the years the game should show the name; where a ruler is named only once or twice the span is a guess and the source says so. A name in brackets means no ruler is recorded for those years: the game should say that rather than invent one. In 'raids', 'where' is a port id from ports_793.json when the place is a port of the game and a plain place name when it is not; 'place' always gives the plain name. Edit freely.

peoples.obodrites: Slavs between the lower Elbe and Wismar bay, with the Wagrians (east Holstein) and Polabians (Ratzeburg) beside them. The Franks' allies against the Saxons, then tributaries of the Saxon dukes. Market: Reric to 808. Chief fort: Mecklenburg.
peoples.wilzi: Slavs east of the Obodrites to the Oder, 'Welatabi in their own tongue' (Einhard). Kings to the 830s; from the 980s the kingless league of the Lutici, with its temple at Rethra. No port in ports_793.json; Menzlin on the Peene was their landing.
peoples.pomeranians: Slavs 'by the sea' from the Oder to the Vistula. No ruler named before 1046. Their great town is Wolin (Jumne) on the Oder mouth. No port in ports_793.json yet.
peoples.prussians: Balts east of the Vistula: Wulfstan's Este, Einhard's Aisti, Adam's Pruzzi and Sembi. A king in every stronghold. Market: Truso.
peoples.curonians: Balts of the coast north of the Prussians: Rimbert's Cori. Five strongholds. Market: Grobin (Seeburg).

rulers.name: Witzan (Witzin)
rulers.title: king of the Obodrites (rex in the Frankish annals)
rulers.how_ended: Killed in a Saxon ambush as he crossed the Elbe at Hliuni (Lüne) on his way to King Charles, 795.
rulers.source: ARF 789 (he marches with Charles against the Wilzi), ARF 795. First named in 789: the start is a guess (?)

rulers.name: Thrasco (Drasco)
rulers.title: duke (dux) of the Obodrites
rulers.seat: not recorded; he is last seen at the emporium of Reric
rulers.how_ended: Driven out by Godfred in 808, back in 809 with Saxon help, then murdered by Godfred's men by a trick at Reric, late 809. A second duke, Godelaib, was taken by a trick and hanged by Godfred in 808.

rulers.name: Sclaomir (Slavomir)
rulers.title: king of the Obodrites
rulers.how_ended: Told in 817 to share the kingship with Thrasco's son Ceadrag, he rose and called in the fleet of Godfred's sons. Brought to Aachen in 819, accused by his own chief men and exiled. Sent home in 821, he fell ill in Saxony, was baptised and died.

rulers.name: Ceadrag
rulers.title: king of the Obodrites, son of Thrasco
rulers.how_ended: Not recorded. Accused of dealing with the Danes in 821, 823 and 826; each time he came to court and kept his rule. Last named in October 826.

rulers.name: (not recorded)
rulers.title: no prince is named in these years
rulers.how_ended: The Obodrites fell away from the Franks in 838 and Saxon counts marched on them in 839.

rulers.name: Goztomuizli (Gostomysl)
rulers.title: king of the Obodrites
rulers.how_ended: Killed when King Louis the German invaded in 844. Louis set the land and people under several dukes.
rulers.source: AF 844; AB 844 (Gestimulus); Ann. Xant. 844. Named only at his death: the start is a guess (?)

rulers.name: (dukes set by King Louis)
rulers.title: several dukes, none named
rulers.how_ended: In 858 an army under the king's son Louis marched against the Obodrites and Linones.

rulers.name: Tabomuizli
rulers.title: duke of the Obodrites
rulers.how_ended: Not recorded. He rebelled in 862; King Louis forced him to submit and to give his son among the hostages. Named only this once.
rulers.source: AF 862

rulers.name: (not recorded)
rulers.title: no prince is named in these years
rulers.how_ended: 889: King Arnulf's campaign fails. 895: Obodrite envoys bring gifts and make peace. 929: tributary to King Henry. 931: Henry has a 'king of the Obodrites' baptised, name not given.
rulers.source: AF 889, 895 (?); Widukind I.36; Continuatio Reginonis 931 (?)

rulers.name: Nakon (Naccon)
rulers.title: prince of the Obodrites; to Ibrahim ibn Yaqub one of the four kings of the Slavs
rulers.seat: Mecklenburg ('the great fort'; Ibrahim's Grad, with a fort in a freshwater lake before it), south of Wismar bay
rulers.how_ended: Died about 965-967, cause not recorded (?). His brother Stoinef was killed at the Raxa on 16 October 955.
rulers.source: Widukind III.50-55; Ibrahim ibn Yaqub (in al-Bakri), about 965; Adam of Bremen II.26

rulers.name: Selibur
rulers.title: under-prince of the Wagrians
rulers.how_ended: Quarrelled with Mstivoj; Duke Hermann Billung judged against him; besieged and starved out in his fort, he lost his rule to his own son.
rulers.source: Widukind III.68. The start is a guess (?)

rulers.name: Mstivoj (Mistui, Mistav)
rulers.title: prince of the Obodrites
rulers.how_ended: Died about 990-995 (?). A Christian with a chaplain, he still burned Hamburg in 983. His daughter Tove married Harald Bluetooth.
rulers.source: Widukind III.68; Thietmar III.18, IV.2; Adam of Bremen II.42 (?); the Sønder Vissing rune stone (DR 55)

rulers.name: Mstislav (Mistizlav)
rulers.title: prince of the Obodrites
rulers.how_ended: In February 1018 the Lutici fell on him for not marching with the emperor the year before. Shut up in Schwerin, then driven out by his own heathen people, he fled to the Bardengau in Saxony.
rulers.source: Thietmar VIII.5; Otto III's charter given at Mecklenburg, 10 September 995 (DO III 172 (?))

rulers.name: Udo (Pribignev)
rulers.title: prince of the Obodrites, 'a bad Christian', beside the heathen princes Gneus and Anatrog
rulers.how_ended: Killed by a Saxon deserter for his cruelty, about 1028 (some put it in 1031 or 1032) (?).
rulers.source: Adam of Bremen II.66

rulers.name: Ratibor
rulers.title: prince of the Slavs (of the Polabians, with the Obodrites under him)
rulers.how_ended: Killed by the Danes in 1043. His eight sons came for revenge and all fell at Lyrskov Heath on 28 September.
rulers.source: Adam of Bremen II.79

rulers.name: Gottschalk (Godescalc)
rulers.title: prince of the Obodrites, Wagrians and Polabians; from 1057 of the Kessini and Circipani too
rulers.seat: Mecklenburg; also Lenzen, Ratzeburg and Old Lübeck
rulers.how_ended: Killed by heathen rebels at Lenzen on 7 June 1066, with the priest Yppo at the altar.
rulers.source: Adam of Bremen II.66, III.19-22, III.50-51; Helmold I.19-22 (written about 1170)

rulers.name: Kruto (Cruto), son of Grin
rulers.title: prince of the Wagrians, then of all the Obodrite lands; a heathen
rulers.how_ended: Killed at a feast about 1090-1093 by the men of Henry, Gottschalk's son. After the game's end.
rulers.source: Helmold I.25-26, 34 (written about 1170)

rulers.name: Dragovit
rulers.title: king of the Wilzi, first among their kings in birth and age
rulers.seat: his own stronghold ('civitas Dragawiti'); its place is not settled: Brandenburg or a fort near the Peene (?)
rulers.how_ended: Not recorded. He came out of his fort to King Charles in 789, gave hostages, swore faith and kept his rule.
rulers.source: ARF 789; ARF rev. 789; Einhard, Vita Karoli 12. Named only in 789: the span is a guess (?)

rulers.name: Liub
rulers.title: king of the Wilzi
rulers.how_ended: Killed in battle against the eastern Obodrites, not long before 823.
rulers.source: ARF 823. Named only at his death: the start is a guess (?)

rulers.name: Milegast
rulers.title: king of the Wilzi, elder son of Liub
rulers.how_ended: Put down by his own people for ruling badly. He and his brother took the quarrel to the emperor at Frankfurt in May 823; Louis asked what the people wanted and confirmed the younger, and sent both home with gifts and under oath.
rulers.source: ARF 823

rulers.name: Cealadrag
rulers.title: king of the Wilzi, younger son of Liub
rulers.how_ended: Not recorded. The Wilzi fell away from the Franks in 838; after that no king of all the Wilzi is ever named again.
rulers.source: ARF 823; AB 838, 839 (?). The end is a guess (?)

rulers.name: (no king named)
rulers.title: the tribes each under their own lords: Redarii, Tollensians, Circipani, Kessini, Ukrani, Hevelli
rulers.how_ended: Made tributary by King Henry in 929, and by Otto and Margrave Gero until 983. The Bavarian Geographer counts 95 strongholds and four regions of the Wilzi.
rulers.source: Bavarian Geographer (9th century); Widukind I.36, II.21, III.53-55

rulers.name: Tugumir
rulers.title: prince of the Hevelli on the Havel (a people beside the Wilzi)
rulers.how_ended: Not recorded. A captive in Saxony since King Henry's day, he was won over by Gero, went home as if escaped, killed his nephew, the last other prince of his house, and handed the fort to King Otto.
rulers.source: Widukind II.21. The end year is a guess (?)

rulers.name: (the assembly of the Lutici)
rulers.title: no lord at all: the Redarii, Tollensians, Circipani and Kessini decide together in assembly
rulers.seat: Rethra (Riedegost), the temple-fort of the Redarii; its place is lost
rulers.how_ended: The league broke in the civil war of 1057; Bishop Burchard of Halberstadt plundered Rethra in the winter of 1067-1068.
rulers.source: Thietmar VI.23-25; Adam of Bremen II.21, III.22; Annales Augustani 1068. The name Lutici is first written in 991 (Annals of Hildesheim) (?)

rulers.name: (no ruler named)
rulers.title: many small tribes; the Wolinians' great town on the Oder mouth is ruled by its elders and has no king
rulers.how_ended: Duke Mieszko of the Polans took the coast to the Oder mouth about 967.
rulers.source: Bavarian Geographer (Velunzani, 70 strongholds; Prissani, 70); Ibrahim ibn Yaqub, about 965

rulers.name: Mieszko I
rulers.title: duke of the Polans, overlord of the Pomeranian coast
rulers.how_ended: Died 25 May 992.
rulers.source: Widukind III.69; Thietmar II.29, IV.58 (?); Ibrahim ibn Yaqub

rulers.name: Bolesław I the Brave
rulers.title: duke of the Polans, overlord of the Pomeranian coast
rulers.seat: Gniezno; his fort at Gdańsk by the Vistula mouth
rulers.how_ended: The western Pomeranians threw off his rule and his bishop about 1005-1007 (?). In 1007 envoys of 'the great city Livilni' (Wolin) were at the emperor's court speaking against him.
rulers.source: Thietmar IV.45, VI.33, VII.72; John Canaparius, Vita Adalberti 27

rulers.name: (no ruler named)
rulers.title: free of the Poles; Wolin its own master
rulers.how_ended: King Magnus of Norway and Denmark besieged Wolin in 1043 and burned much of it.
rulers.source: Thietmar VI.33; Adam of Bremen II.22, II.79 and its scholion

rulers.name: Zemuzil
rulers.title: duke of the Pomeranians (dux Bomeraniorum)
rulers.how_ended: Not recorded. Named once, when he came to King Henry III at Merseburg at midsummer 1046 beside the dukes of the Bohemians and the Poles.
rulers.source: Annales Altahenses maiores 1046

rulers.name: (not recorded)
rulers.title: dukes of the Pomeranians, none named; the eastern part pays the duke of the Poles after 1047 (?)
rulers.source: Gallus Anonymus I.20-21 (written about 1115)

rulers.name: (no single ruler)
rulers.title: a king in every stronghold
rulers.seat: many strongholds; the market is Truso on Lake Drużno
rulers.source: Wulfstan in the Old English Orosius, about 890; Adam of Bremen IV.18 (they will have no master over them)

rulers.name: Netimer
rulers.title: a king on the border of Prussia, Rus and Lithuania; perhaps a Yotvingian rather than a Prussian (?)
rulers.how_ended: Not recorded. He let Bruno of Querfurt baptise him; his brother's men then killed Bruno.
rulers.source: Wibert's account of Bruno's death (11th century) (?); Annales Quedlinburgenses 1009

rulers.name: (no single ruler)
rulers.title: a land of five strongholds (civitates), each its own
rulers.seat: Seeburg (taken to be Grobiņa) and Apulia (Apuolė)
rulers.how_ended: Once under the Svear and long since free of them; made to pay the Svear again about 854, for how long is not known.
rulers.source: Rimbert, Vita Anskarii 30; Adam of Bremen IV.16

overlords.what: allies, then clients: gifts, hostages, and the prince made or confirmed at the emperor's court
two thirds of the people pay him tribute; before 808 Reric's toll was already his
hostages and tribute in the years he can enforce it (844, 862); not in 889

overlords.who: the Saxon king, then the Billung dukes of Saxony
overlords.what: yearly tribute; heavier under Duke Bernhard II, which Adam blames for the risings
overlords.source: Widukind I.36, III.68; Adam of Bremen II.48 (?), III.22-23

overlords.what: hostages and oaths; in 808-812 they side with the Danes

overlords.who: the Saxon king, through Margrave Gero and his heirs
overlords.what: tribute in silver, a tenth of it to Saint Maurice at Magdeburg
overlords.source: Widukind I.36, II.21; Otto I's charters for Magdeburg (?)

overlords.what: free; from 1003 the emperor's heathen allies, paying nothing
tribute again, raised in 1036 and promised again in 1045; thrown off after the victory of 1056
tribute, his forts at the river mouths, and from 1000 his bishop at Kołobrzeg
a ransom, tribute as of old and thirty hostages; how long it was paid is not known

wars.who: Charlemagne with Franks, Saxons, Sorbs, the Obodrites under Witzan and Frisians in ships, against the Wilzi under Dragovit
wars.what: The king bridges the Elbe and marches to the Peene; the Frisians come up the Havel by ship to join him. Dragovit gives hostages and swears faith. Einhard says the war was made because the Wilzi kept harrying the Obodrites.
wars.what_it_did_to_trade: Before the game's start, and the root of what follows: the Obodrites are the king's friends, the Wilzi his sworn men, and Frisian skippers know the Elbe and the Havel.
wars.source: ARF 789; ARF rev. 789; Einhard, Vita Karoli 12

wars.who: the Saxons beyond the Elbe against the Obodrites, the king's allies
wars.what: Witzan is killed at the Elbe crossing in 795. In 798 Thrasco, with the king's envoy Eburis, destroys the Nordalbingian Saxons on the Suentana field (Bornhöved): 4,000 dead by the royal annals.
wars.what_it_did_to_trade: The Obodrites are masters from the Elbe to the Danish border, and Reric has captives and plunder to sell (?).

wars.who: Charlemagne against the last Saxons beyond the Elbe; the Obodrites as his heirs there
wars.what: The king camps at Hollenstedt, has the Saxons of Wigmodia and of the land beyond the Elbe carried off into Francia, and gives that land to the Obodrites. Thrasco comes to the camp with gifts. Godfred lies at Sliesthorp with his fleet and horsemen and will not come to meet the king.
wars.what_it_did_to_trade: For six years the Obodrite prince is master from Wismar bay to the Danish border, with the emperor's leave: one peace covers the whole road from the Elbe to Reric. The Saxons get the land back about 810.
wars.source: ARF 804; Chron. Moiss. 804; Einhard, Vita Karoli 7 (in chronicle_793.json)

wars.who: Godfred, king of the Danes, with the Wilzi, against the Obodrites and the Franks
wars.what: Godfred storms Obodrite forts, makes two thirds of the people pay him, hangs Duke Godelaib, drives out Thrasco, destroys Reric and carries its merchants to Sliesthorp. The Linones and Smeldingi go over to him; Charles the Younger bridges the Elbe and burns their land. In 809 Thrasco comes back with Saxons, wastes the Wilzi and storms the Smeldingi's chief fort, and is murdered at Reric. In 810 the Wilzi take the Elbe fort of Hohbuoki; Godfred is killed by one of his own men.
wars.what_it_did_to_trade: Reric is finished as the Wends' market. Its merchants and its toll sit at Sliesthorp behind the Danish king's new wall, which has one gate for carts and riders. A Wend sells in a Danish harbour from now on.
wars.source: ARF 808, 809, 810; Chron. Moiss. 808-810; Einhard, Vita Karoli 14

wars.who: the Franks and Saxons against the Linones and the Wilzi
wars.what: In 811 an army wastes the Linones and rebuilds Hohbuoki. In 812 three armies enter the Wilzi land and take hostages.
wars.what_it_did_to_trade: The middle Elbe crossing is the king's again and the border posts work.

wars.who: the Saxon counts and the Obodrites, for the emperor, against the sons of Godfred
wars.what: By the emperor's order all the Saxon counts and the Obodrite levy cross the Eider with the envoy Baldric to put the exile Harald back. They camp seven days in Sinlendi; the Danes keep to their 200 ships off an island and will not fight. The army burns the country round, takes forty hostages and goes home.
wars.what_it_did_to_trade: The Obodrites march as the emperor's men against the Danish king whose harbour they must sell in. Sliesthorp is no place for a Wend or a Frank that summer.

wars.who: Sclaomir of the Obodrites and the sons of Godfred against the emperor
wars.what: Sclaomir will not share his kingship with Ceadrag. A Danish fleet comes up the Elbe to the fort of Esesfeld on the Stör and burns the river bank while Danes and Obodrites come by land; the fort holds. In 819 the Saxon border commanders bring Sclaomir to Aachen.
wars.what_it_did_to_trade: Danish warships in the Elbe mouth in 817: the way to Hamburg and Bardowick is not safe that summer.

wars.who: the Obodrites and Wilzi against the Franks
wars.what: Both peoples fall away while the emperor's sons fight him. Saxon counts are sent against the Obodrites and Linones in 839.
wars.what_it_did_to_trade: The Elbe posts are a war border again; nobody at court has time for a merchant's complaint.

wars.who: Louis the German against the Obodrites
wars.what: The king invades, King Goztomuizli is killed, and the land is put under several dukes.
wars.what_it_did_to_trade: One prince's peace becomes several dukes' peaces: more hands to fill on the way from the Elbe to the coast.

wars.who: the Danes, then the Svear under King Olof, against the Curonians
wars.what: A Danish fleet is beaten: half the men killed, half the ships taken with their gold, silver and spoil. The next year Olof burns Seeburg, said to hold 7,000 fighting men, marches five days to Apulia, said to hold 15,000, and besieges it eight days until it buys peace.
wars.what_it_did_to_trade: Grobin is burned. Afterwards the Curonians pay the Svear, and Svear and Gotland men trade there under their king's name; a Dane is last year's enemy.
wars.source: Rimbert, Vita Anskarii 30. The years are about 853-854 (?)

wars.who: Louis the German and his son Louis against the Obodrites and Linones
wars.what: An army under the younger Louis in 858; in 862 the king forces the rebel duke Tabomuizli to give his son and other hostages.
wars.what_it_did_to_trade: Tribute and hostages keep the Elbe posts open in the king's good years.

wars.who: King Arnulf against the Obodrites
wars.what: Arnulf's campaign of 889 gains nothing. In 895 Obodrite envoys come to him with gifts and peace is made.
wars.what_it_did_to_trade: For forty years after this no king can force the Wends: they are free, and so are their tolls.

wars.who: King Henry I of the East Franks against the Hevelli, Redarii and all the Elbe Slavs
wars.what: In a hard winter Henry camps on the ice and takes Brandenburg by hunger, sword and cold. Obodrites, Wilzi, Hevelli and Redarii are made tributary. The Redarii rise, storm Walsleben and kill everyone in it. On 4 September 929 the Saxons destroy the Slav army at Lenzen; the captives are beheaded the next day.
wars.what_it_did_to_trade: Tribute in silver from every people as far as the Oder goes west each year, and the Saxon lords have captives to sell. Stay off the middle Elbe in 929.
wars.source: Widukind I.35-36; Thietmar I.10; Annales Corbeienses 929 (?)

wars.who: Otto I, Hermann Billung and Margrave Gero against the Redarii, Hevelli and Obodrites
wars.what: Hermann Billung beats the Redarii in 936. In 939 Gero, warned of a plot, has about thirty Slav princes killed drunk at a feast; the tribes rise and destroy a Saxon army. Tugumir then betrays Brandenburg, and all the peoples to the Oder pay tribute.
wars.what_it_did_to_trade: From 940 one margrave's word runs from the Elbe to the Oder. The posts of 805 turn into markets: Magdeburg above all.

wars.who: the Saxon rebel Wichmann with the Obodrite brothers Nakon and Stoinef, against Otto I, Hermann Billung and Gero
wars.what: The Ukrani are beaten in 954. In 955 the Obodrites take a Saxon fort on terms and then kill its men. On 16 October 955 Otto crosses the Raxa (Recknitz) with Gero's help; Stoinef is killed in flight, his head set up on the field and 700 captives beheaded round it. War with the Redarii goes on to 960.
wars.what_it_did_to_trade: The slave markets are full after 955. Nakon keeps his rule by paying, and for a generation the Obodrite land is the quietest part of the coast.
wars.source: Widukind III.42, III.50-55; Thietmar II.12; Annals of St Gall 955

wars.who: Wichmann with the Redarii and the Wolinians, against Duke Mieszko of the Polans
wars.what: Wichmann beats Mieszko twice in 963 and kills his brother. In 967 Mieszko, with two troops of Bohemian horsemen, draws the Wolinians on by a feigned flight and breaks them; Wichmann is killed at dawn on 22 September, giving up his sword to be carried to the emperor.
wars.what_it_did_to_trade: The Oder mouth comes under the Polish duke. Wolin keeps its trade and its own elders, and has one more lord to satisfy.

wars.who: Duke Hermann Billung and Mstivoj of the Obodrites against Selibur of the Wagrians
wars.what: The two princes had an old feud. Hermann finds for Mstivoj and fines Selibur, who takes up arms, is shut in his fort without stores and gives up. A bronze idol is found in the plunder; Selibur's son rules in his place.
wars.what_it_did_to_trade: Starigard is the duke's from now on; a bishop is set there within a few years.

wars.who: Margrave Hodo against Duke Mieszko
wars.what: On 24 June 972 Hodo attacks Mieszko at Cidini (Cedynia) on the lower Oder and loses nearly all his knights. The emperor orders both to keep the peace until he comes home.
wars.what_it_did_to_trade: The lower Oder stays Polish: its tribute is the duke's to pay to the emperor, not the margrave's to take.

wars.who: the Lutici and Obodrites against the Saxons
wars.what: In the summer of 983 the Lutici storm Havelberg (29 June) and Brandenburg (three days later); Mstivoj burns Hamburg and the Obodrites burn the monastery at Kalbe. A Saxon army stops them on the Tanger. Then a war every year: Saxon and Polish armies in the Slav land in 985-987, fights for Brandenburg in 991-993, Otto III at Mecklenburg in 995, the last great campaign in 997.
wars.what_it_did_to_trade: East of the Elbe the bishops, the tribute and the Saxon merchants are gone for good in the Lutici land. Magdeburg lives on as a border market. The coast towns, above all Wolin, trade on with Danes, Rus and Poles.
wars.source: Thietmar III.17-19, IV.11-13, IV.19, IV.29 (?); Annals of Hildesheim and Quedlinburg 985-997 (?)

wars.who: Harald Bluetooth, king of the Danes, against his son Sweyn
wars.what: Beaten and wounded, Harald flees by ship to Jumne (Wolin), 'the city of the Slavs', and dies there within days.
wars.what_it_did_to_trade: Wolin shelters a Danish king and his ships: Danes are at home in the town. Later saga makes it the nest of the Jomsvikings; that is saga only.
wars.source: Adam of Bremen II.27-28; Jómsvíkinga saga (about 1200, not history). The year is 986 or 987 (?)

wars.who: Sweyn of the Danes, Olof of the Svear and Jarl Eirik against Olaf Tryggvason of Norway
wars.what: Olaf is caught at sea and beaten, and leaps from his ship. Adam puts the fight in the Øresund. The sagas put it 'by Svolder' off the Wendish coast, with Olaf sailing home from Wendland and a Wendish king Burislav in the tale; that part is saga only.
wars.what_it_did_to_trade: If the sagas have the place right, three kings' fleets lay in the Wendish sounds late that summer. The Wends took no side that any source of the time records.
wars.source: Adam of Bremen II.40; Snorri, Óláfs saga Tryggvasonar (about 1230, not history for the place) (?); chronicle_793.json 1000-09-09-svolder

wars.who: King Henry II with the Lutici, against Bolesław of the Poles
wars.what: At Quedlinburg at Easter 1003 the king makes friends of the Redarii and Lutici. They march with him in 1005, 1015 and 1017 behind their gods' banners. In 1007 envoys of the Lutici, of Wolin and of Bohemia warn the king against Bolesław at Regensburg.
wars.what_it_did_to_trade: The Lutici land is open to Saxons again, as allies' land without tribute. The war shuts the Oder road between Saxony and the Poles in the campaign years.
wars.source: Thietmar V.31, VI.22-25, VI.33, VII.64; Bruno of Querfurt's letter to Henry II (1008)

wars.who: the Lutici and the heathen Obodrites against Prince Mstislav
wars.what: In February the Lutici attack Mstislav for not helping the emperor in 1017. His own people turn on him; he is shut in Schwerin and driven out. The churches are burned and Bishop Bernhard of Oldenburg flees to the emperor.
wars.what_it_did_to_trade: No Christian prince holds the Obodrite land for ten years. The Saxon dukes take their tribute and ask nothing about the faith.

wars.who: Gottschalk, Udo's son, against the Saxons of Nordalbingia
wars.what: Hearing his father is killed, Gottschalk leaves the school at Lüneburg, crosses the Elbe, gathers Slavs and kills Saxons through Holstein and Stormarn, until Duke Bernhard takes him. Freed, he goes to King Cnut and serves him in England.
wars.what_it_did_to_trade: The road from Hamburg to Oldenburg and the Trave is closed by robbers for some years.
wars.source: Adam of Bremen II.66. The years are about 1028-1030 (?)

wars.who: Emperor Conrad II against the Lutici
wars.what: The Lutici attack the fort of Werben on the Elbe in 1033 and take it in 1035. Conrad comes through the marshes, fighting on foot, and has captives maimed as they had maimed a crucifix. In 1036 the Lutici give hostages and a heavier tribute.
wars.what_it_did_to_trade: The middle Elbe is unsafe for three years; then Lutici silver goes west again.
wars.source: Wipo, Gesta Chuonradi 33; Annals of Hildesheim 1033-1036 (?)

wars.who: Magnus, king of Norway and Denmark, against the Wends
wars.what: Magnus besieges Jumne (Wolin) with a great fleet and burns much of it. Ratibor is killed by the Danes. A Wendish army that had wasted Jutland as far as Ribe is caught on Lyrskov Heath on 28 September and cut down; Ratibor's eight sons die there.
wars.what_it_did_to_trade: Wolin never fully recovers; its trade drifts to Szczecin and Kamień in the next lifetime. The Wendish sea-raids on Jutland stop for a while, and Gottschalk comes home to rule.
wars.source: Adam of Bremen II.79 and scholion; Snorri, Magnúss saga góða (about 1230)

wars.who: King Henry III against the Lutici
wars.what: The king marches; the Lutici submit and promise the old tribute.
wars.what_it_did_to_trade: Eleven quiet years on the middle Elbe.

wars.who: Duke Casimir of the Poles, with Rus help, against Miecław of Mazovia and the Pomeranians
wars.what: Casimir destroys Miecław, then beats the Pomeranians who were coming to help him.
wars.what_it_did_to_trade: The eastern Pomeranians by the Vistula pay the Polish duke again; Gdańsk is his fort.

wars.who: the Lutici against the Saxons under Margrave William of the Nordmark
wars.what: On 10 September 1056 the Saxon army is destroyed at Pritzlawa, where the Havel meets the Elbe; the margrave falls with many nobles. The emperor dies a month later.
wars.what_it_did_to_trade: The Lutici pay nobody. The middle Elbe is a war border until the game ends.
wars.source: Annales Altahenses maiores 1056 (?); Lampert of Hersfeld 1056 (?). The day is from memory (?)

wars.who: Lutici against Lutici: the Kessini and Circipani against the Redarii and Tollensians; then Gottschalk, Duke Bernhard of Saxony and King Sweyn of the Danes
wars.what: The Redarii and Tollensians, three times beaten, call in the three princes, who fight the Circipani for seven weeks until they buy peace for 15,000 pounds of silver. Adam adds that of the faith not a word was said.
wars.what_it_did_to_trade: The league that kept the Lutici land closed is broken. Gottschalk now rules to the Peene, and one man's peace runs from the Trave to Demmin.

wars.who: the heathen Obodrites and Lutici against Gottschalk and the church
wars.what: Gottschalk is killed at Lenzen on 7 June. The monks of Ratzeburg are stoned on 15 July. Old Bishop John of Mecklenburg is taken, and his head offered to the god at Rethra on 10 November. Gottschalk's widow, the Danish king's daughter, is driven out naked from Mecklenburg. Hamburg is wasted and Schleswig destroyed.
wars.what_it_did_to_trade: The old harbour at Sliesthorp is burned and the Christian merchants' road from Hamburg to the Baltic is cut. The Wends hold everything east of the Limes for two more lifetimes.
wars.source: Adam of Bremen III.50-51; Helmold I.22-24 (about 1170)

wars.who: Bishop Burchard of Halberstadt, then King Henry IV, against the Lutici
wars.what: In the winter of 1067-1068 Burchard rides into the Lutici land, burns and wastes it, and rides home on the sacred horse that was honoured as a god at Rethra. Henry IV plunders the land again in the winter of 1069.
wars.what_it_did_to_trade: Just past the game's end. The temple that had spoken for the Lutici is shamed and never named again.

raids.what: The emporium is destroyed and its merchants put aboard the king's ships and set down at Sliesthorp. The annals say its tolls had paid him well.
Thrasco, duke of the Obodrites, is killed by a trick at the emporium, which is plainly still in use a year after it was 'destroyed'.
The king's fort on the Elbe is taken with its garrison of East Saxons under the envoy Odo.

raids.who: Sclaomir's Obodrites and the fleet of Godfred's sons
raids.what: The fleet comes up the Elbe and burns the banks of the Stör; the fort is besieged from land and water and holds.
A Danish fleet comes to plunder and is beaten: half the men are killed and half the ships taken, with gold, silver and spoil.

raids.place: Seeburg (taken to be Grobiņa), then Apulia (Apuolė)
raids.what: Seeburg is plundered and burned. At Apulia, after eight days, the Curonians offer the gold and arms taken from the Danes, half a pound of silver for each man in the fort, the old tribute and thirty hostages. Christian merchants in the Svear army had urged the lot be cast for Christ's help.

raids.who: Egil Skallagrimsson and his brother Thorolf (saga)
raids.what: The saga has them make a fortnight's peace with the Curonians to hold a market, and raid as soon as it ran out; Egil is taken at a farm, breaks out with a chest of silver and burns the hall. A story, but the truce-market is how such coasts were worked.
raids.source: Egils saga 46 (written about 1230; the year is the saga's reckoning, uncertain) (?)

raids.what: The fort is stormed and everyone in it killed; the signal for a general rising, ended at Lenzen on 4 September.

raids.who: the Obodrites under Nakon and Stoinef, with the Saxon rebel Wichmann
raids.what: The garrison gives up on a promise of life; a quarrel breaks out, the grown men are killed and the women and children carried off.

Havelberg's garrison is killed and the bishop's church wrecked on 29 June; three days later Brandenburg falls at the first bell of morning, the bishop having fled. The clergy are taken, a dead bishop's grave is robbed and the church treasure carried off.

raids.place: Hamburg; the monastery of Saint Laurence at Kalbe
raids.what: Hamburg is plundered and burned, and the monastery at Kalbe burned.
raids.source: Thietmar III.18; Adam of Bremen II.42-43 (his dating is confused) (?)

raids.what: While the emperor is in the Hevelli land the Lutici raid west of the Elbe and are beaten by a Westphalian force led by a bishop.
The market ends in fire: burned buildings and arrowheads in the ash. The dig dates it only roughly, to the later 10th century or about 1000; some think a Polish duke's men did it. No written source.
raids.source: The excavations at Janów Pomorski (M. Jagodziński; M. Bogucki) (?)

raids.who: the Lutici and the heathen Obodrites
raids.what: Prince Mstislav is besieged in Schwerin and driven out; every church in the land is burned and the crosses cut down.
Avenging his father, he kills and robs through the Saxon land beyond the Elbe until the duke takes him.
The border fort, attacked again and again since 1033, is taken and its garrison killed or carried off.
A great Wendish army wastes Jutland up to Ribe; on its way home King Magnus meets it on Lyrskov Heath near Hedeby on 28 September.

raids.who: Magnus, king of Norway and Denmark
raids.what: The 'richest city of the Slavs' is besieged from the sea and much of it burned; the fort in the middle is not taken (?).
raids.source: Adam of Bremen II.79, scholion; Snorri, Magnúss saga góða (about 1230)

raids.what: Lenzen on 7 June, Ratzeburg on 15 July, then Mecklenburg; Hamburg is plundered and its fort pulled down.
The rich town on the Danish border, full of merchants, is attacked without warning and destroyed.
A winter ride into the Lutici land: the country is burned and the god's horse taken and ridden home.

raids.who: Curonians, Sembians and other men of the east shore
raids.what: Sea-raiders from the east coast trouble the Danes in King Sweyn Estridsen's last years; his son Cnut makes his name fighting them. Only later writers say so.
raids.source: Ælnoth, Gesta Swenomagni (about 1120) (?); Knýtlinga saga (about 1250) (?). The year is rough

laws.what: The king's law since Herstal, said again in 803 and 805: no mail coat goes out of the realm, and none is to be sold to a merchant.
laws.what_it_means_for_a_merchant: A Frankish sword or byrnie is worth most among the Wends and is the one thing you may not carry there. If it is found, everything you have is taken.
laws.source: Capitulary of Herstal (779) c. 20; MGH Capit. I no. 40 c. 7 (803) (?), no. 44 c. 7 (805)

laws.what: Thionville: merchants going to the Slavs may go no further than the named posts, each under a king's man. On this border: Bardowick (under Hredi), Schezla (under Madalgaud) and Magdeburg (under Aito).
laws.what_it_means_for_a_merchant: You may not cross the Elbe to trade. The Wends come to Bardowick and Magdeburg; you sell there, under the envoy's eye, and no arms. By sea nobody has written a rule.
laws.source: MGH Capit. I no. 44 c. 7 (in chronicle_793.json)

laws.what: Godfred moves the merchants of Reric to Sliesthorp and orders a wall across the neck of Jutland from the eastern bay to the western sea, with a single gate for carts and riders.
laws.what_it_means_for_a_merchant: Wendish wax, honey and captives are now bought at Sliesthorp, and the toll on them is the Danish king's. Goods crossing between the two seas pass his one gate.

laws.what: The Saxons get back the land beyond the Elbe that the Obodrites were given in 804, and a border is drawn from the Elbe near Boizenburg north to the Kiel fjord: the Limes Saxoniae.
laws.what_it_means_for_a_merchant: West of the line the count's toll and Saxon law; east of it the Wendish prince's. The line holds, on parchment at least, to the end of the game.
laws.source: Adam of Bremen II.18 (he copies an old boundary deed); ARF 809-811 (the fort at Esesfeld). The year is about 810 (?)

laws.what: The emperor judges between kings of the Wends: the Wilzi brothers Milegast and Cealadrag at Frankfurt in 823; the Obodrite Ceadrag summoned in 821, 823 and 826 on his own people's charges.
laws.what_it_means_for_a_merchant: A Wendish prince answers to the palace. A wrong done to a king's merchant can be carried to court, and the prince knows it (?).

laws.what: The Curonians of Apulia buy peace from the Svear: the Danish plunder, half a pound of silver a head, the old tribute, thirty hostages.
laws.what_it_means_for_a_merchant: A ship from Birka or Gotland is among the lords' own men on the Curonian coast. A ship out of Sliesthorp is not.

laws.what: The custom of the Este, as Wulfstan saw it. A king in every stronghold. The king and the rich drink mare's milk, the poor and the slaves mead; no ale is brewed. A dead man lies unburned in his house a month or two, a king half a year, while his kin drink and play; they can keep him cold. On the burning day what is left of his goods is set out in five or six heaps along a mile, the largest furthest off, and the men with the fastest horses ride for them.
laws.what_it_means_for_a_merchant: No one king can give you peace for the whole land: you deal fort by fort. A dead partner's goods go to the best horse, not to his heirs or his creditors. Bring no ale to sell; a fast horse fetches any price.
laws.source: Wulfstan's report in the Old English Orosius (about 890)

laws.what: All the Slav peoples from the Elbe to the Oder pay the Saxon king a yearly tribute, taken by the margraves; from 937 a tenth of it goes to the monastery of Saint Maurice at Magdeburg.
laws.what_it_means_for_a_merchant: Silver the Wends earn on the coast goes west as tribute, and the lords who take it want things to spend it on. In force until 983; for the Obodrites, to the dukes, until 1066.
laws.source: Widukind I.36, II.21; Otto I's foundation charter for Magdeburg, 21 September 937 (DO I 14) (?)

laws.what: Otto I gives Saint Maurice at Magdeburg the market, the mint and the toll there, and the lordship over the Jews and other merchants who live in the place.
laws.what_it_means_for_a_merchant: At Magdeburg you pay the church's toll, trade in its pennies and take your case to its advocate. It is the great gate to the Wends by land.

laws.what: Ibrahim ibn Yaqub on the Wends. Nakon's land is cheap to live in and rich in horses, which are sent abroad; his men have mail, helmets and swords. The people with the great town by the sea (Wolin) have no king and are ruled by their elders. Mieszko takes his dues in market weights and pays his three thousand mailed men with them.
laws.what_it_means_for_a_merchant: Buy horses of the Obodrites. At Wolin there is no king's reeve to buy: the elders keep the harbour and its rules. Among the Poles the duke's toll is weighed, not counted.
laws.source: Ibrahim ibn Yaqub in al-Bakri, Kitab al-masalik wa'l-mamalik (about 965)

laws.what: Otto II confirms to the merchants of Magdeburg that they pay no toll anywhere in his realm, save at Mainz, Cologne, Tiel and Bardowick.
laws.what_it_means_for_a_merchant: A Magdeburg man undersells you everywhere but at those four tolls. Tiel, the Frisians' own river town, is one of the four.

laws.what: The Prussians' answer to Bishop Adalbert at the market place: this land, 'of which we are the gate', has one law and one way of living; men of another law must be gone by night or lose their heads.
laws.what_it_means_for_a_merchant: The Prussian shore is open to a man who comes to trade and shut to one who brings a priest. Do not carry preachers, whatever the duke at Gdańsk pays.
laws.source: John Canaparius, Vita Adalberti 28; Bruno of Querfurt, Vita Adalberti 25 (?)

laws.what: King Henry II takes the Lutici as allies at Quedlinburg at Easter. They keep their gods and pay no tribute.
laws.what_it_means_for_a_merchant: A Saxon may go among the Lutici again, as the guest of allies. There is still no church and no lord's court there.
laws.source: Thietmar V.31; Bruno of Querfurt's letter to Henry II (1008)

laws.what: The law of the Lutici, as Thietmar wrote it. No one lord rules. All matters are settled in assembly and all must agree; a man who speaks against is beaten with rods, and if he resists outside the meeting he loses everything by fire and plunder or pays a fine by his rank. Peace is made by offering a lock cut from the crown of the head with a tuft of grass, and giving the right hand. War and peace are asked of the gods by lot and by the sacred horse at Rethra.
laws.what_it_means_for_a_merchant: There is nobody to buy a charter from. Your safety is the assembly's word and a host who will answer for you. A peace sworn their way is kept.

laws.what: The Lutici give Conrad II hostages and a tribute raised above the old one.
laws.what_it_means_for_a_merchant: For twenty years the Lutici need silver every year, and sell honey, wax, furs and people to get it.

laws.what: The rule of Jumne (Wolin), as Adam heard it: the town is open to all the peoples round about, Slavs, 'Greeks' (men of the Rus church) and barbarians; Saxons too may live there as long as they do not show their Christian faith. A fire, 'Vulcan's pot', burns as a mark for ships. He calls the people as honest and open-handed to guests as any on earth.
laws.what_it_means_for_a_merchant: Keep the cross inside your shirt and you may trade and even settle. A stranger is safe in a man's house there.
laws.source: Adam of Bremen II.22 (written about 1075, of the town before and after 1043)

laws.what: The Sembi or Pruzzi, as Adam heard it: they go out to help men in danger at sea or set on by pirates; they care little for gold and silver; they have furs in plenty and give marten skins for the woollen cloaks called faldones; no Christian may come near their groves and springs; they will have no master.
laws.what_it_means_for_a_merchant: Bring woollen cloth, not coin, and take furs and amber. A wreck on their shore is not plundered. Keep away from a grove.

coins.what: No ruler of the Obodrites, Wilzi, Pomeranians, Prussians or Curonians strikes a coin in the game's years. Silver goes by weight; the first Wendish coins are of the 12th century (?).
coins.source: The hoards of the south Baltic coast (Kiersnowski; Herrmann, Die Slawen in Deutschland) (?)

coins.what: At Reric a few small silver pennies of the North Sea kind (sceattas of the Ribe 'Wodan and monster' type) and Frankish deniers pass among the foreign traders (?).

Dirhams: the caliphs' silver, first Abbasid, from about 900 Samanid, come by the Rus rivers. Whole and cut, by weight. Truso has given hundreds of loose dirhams, most struck before about 850 (?); the hoard at Ralswiek on Rügen held some 2,200, the latest of the 840s. The flow thins from about 965 and ends in the 1010s.
coins.source: The Ralswiek hoard (Stralsund museum: some 2,200 dirhams; the latest is put at 842 or 847 (?)); the Truso finds (Bogucki) (?); chronicle_793.json 1000-silver-fades

coins.what: The first Danish pennies of Hedeby turn up in ones and twos on the south coast and at Truso (?).
coins.source: Malmer on the Hedeby coinage; the Truso finds (?)

coins.what: Hack-silver and the folding scale. Every trader carries a balance in a case and a set of weights (small bronze cubes with the corners cut, iron balls cased in bronze); arm-rings and coins are cut into ever smaller bits, and a penny's worth is a snip.
coins.source: Scales and weights from Truso, Wolin and Menzlin; Steuer on the weight economy (?)

coins.what: Saxon pennies with a raised rim (later called Wendish pennies): a cross on one side, a church on the other, strokes instead of letters, about a gram and a half, made for the trade east of the Elbe. They fill the hoards of the Wends and Pomeranians.
coins.source: Coin study of the Sachsenpfennig type (struck about 940 to 1105)

coins.what: The archbishop's pennies at Magdeburg and the Billung dukes' pennies at Bardowick and Lüneburg: what a merchant is paid in at the Elbe markets.
Otto-and-Adelheid pennies, of the new Harz silver, by the thousand in the coast hoards; with them English pennies of Æthelred and Cnut and Danish copies, come east with the tribute money.
coins.source: Coin study of the Otto-Adelheid pennies (from about 983-984); the Pomeranian hoards (?)

coins.what: A few pennies in the name of Bolesław of the Poles, for show more than for trade; on the coast they are silver by weight like any other.
coins.source: Suchodolski on the first Polish coinage (?)

coins.what: Cloth as money. Ibrahim saw small thin cloths of no other use passing as coin among the Slavs at Prague; Helmold, a century after the game, says the Rani of Rügen have no coin and buy everything with linen cloth.
coins.source: Ibrahim ibn Yaqub in al-Bakri; Helmold I.38 (about 1170)

church.what: No church among any of the five peoples. The Wends keep their gods in groves and forts; the Prussians and Curonians burn their dead and ask the lot.
church.source: Einhard, Vita Karoli 12; Wulfstan; Rimbert, Vita Anskarii 30

church.what: Sclaomir, the deposed king of the Obodrites, is baptised on his sickbed in Saxony and dies: the first Obodrite prince known to be christened.
Hamburg is made the see for the north; Ansgar is the pope's envoy to the Swedes, the Danes and the Slavs. He buys Danish and Slav boys to bring up as clerks.
Hamburg, the only church on the Wends' border, is burned by a Danish fleet; the see is joined to Bremen.

Before Apulia the Svear cast lots and find none of their gods will help; Christian merchants in the army say call on Christ, and the lot falls for it. After the victory the heathen Svear keep a fast in his honour.
King Henry has a king of the Obodrites baptised, with a king of the Danes.
Otto I founds the monastery of Saint Maurice at Magdeburg, with a tenth of the Slav tribute.
Bishops are set at Havelberg and Brandenburg in the Wilzi and Hevelli lands.
church.source: Otto I's foundation charters (Brandenburg, 1 October 948; both dates are disputed) (?)

church.what: A bronze idol is found in the plunder of Selibur's fort and shown to the people as a sight.

Magdeburg is made an archbishop's see for the Slavs beyond the Elbe. A bishop is set at Oldenburg (Starigard) for the Obodrites, under Hamburg; Adam was told that of eighteen districts of the Slavs all but three were then baptised.
church.source: Thietmar II.22; Adam of Bremen II.16, II.26. Oldenburg's year is about 968-972 (?)

church.what: The sees of Havelberg and Brandenburg are destroyed, their clergy killed or enslaved. No bishop sits in either again inside the game's years.

Adalbert, once bishop of Prague, baptises a crowd at Gdańsk, sails to the Prussians with two companions, is struck with an oar at his first landing, told to leave at the market, and killed on 23 April. Duke Bolesław buys the body back (for its weight in gold, a later tale says) and lays it at Gniezno.
church.source: John Canaparius, Vita Adalberti 27-30 (about 999); Bruno of Querfurt, Vita Adalberti (1004)

church.what: At Gniezno, over Adalbert's grave, the emperor and Bolesław set up an archbishop and a bishop for the Pomeranians at Kołobrzeg, the salt town: Reinbern, who burns the idol houses and throws four stones anointed with oil into the sea to cleanse it.

The Pomeranians throw off the Poles and the bishop; the see of Kołobrzeg is not heard of again. In the same year the heathen Lutici march in the Christian king's army behind their idols, and Thietmar describes Rethra: a three-cornered fort with three gates in a holy wood, a wooden temple set on the horns of beasts, armed images with their names cut on them, the chief called Zuarasici.
church.source: Thietmar VI.22-25; the Pomeranian date is about 1005-1007 (?)

church.what: Bruno of Querfurt, missionary archbishop, is beheaded with eighteen companions on the border of Prussia, Rus and Lithuania, on 9 March (or 14 February).

The Obodrites drive out their Christian prince and burn the churches; Bishop Bernhard of Oldenburg flees. Adam tells of sixty priests at Oldenburg led about with a cross cut into their scalps, though he puts it earlier.
church.source: Thietmar VIII.5-6; Adam of Bremen II.43 (?)

church.what: Gottschalk comes home a Christian and a soldier of King Cnut. He builds churches and stands up in them to say in the Slav tongue what the priests have said in theirs.

Archbishop Adalbert of Hamburg sets bishops in Gottschalk's land: Mecklenburg (John, an old Irishman), Ratzeburg (Aristo, who had been to Jerusalem) and Oldenburg (Ezzo). There are houses of canons, monks or nuns at Lübeck, Oldenburg, Ratzeburg and Lenzen, and three at Mecklenburg.
church.source: Adam of Bremen III.20-21. The year is about 1060-1062 (?)

church.what: The priest Yppo is killed on the altar at Lenzen with Gottschalk (7 June); the monk Ansverus and his brothers are stoned at Ratzeburg (15 July); Bishop John is beaten, led round the forts, his hands and feet cut off and his head carried on a spear to the god at Rethra (10 November).
Bishop Burchard of Halberstadt rides home from Rethra on the god's sacred horse.

One church stands in Courland, built by a merchant whom the king of the Danes won to it with many gifts; the king told Adam so himself. Adam says the Curonians' houses are full of soothsayers whom men come from far to consult.

The Rani of Rügen and their temple at Arkona are heathen to the end of the game and long after (the temple falls in 1168). A tale that monks of Corvey once preached Saint Vitus to them is told only in the 12th century.
church.source: Helmold I.6, II.12 (about 1170); Widukind III.54 names the Rani in 955

sources.ARF: Annales regni Francorum, by year entry; ARF rev. is the revised version
sources.Wulfstan: his report of the voyage from Hedeby to Truso, added to the Old English Orosius at Alfred's court, about 890
sources.Bavarian Geographer: Descriptio civitatum et regionum ad septentrionalem plagam Danubii, a 9th-century list of peoples and their strongholds
sources.Widukind: Widukind of Corvey, Res gestae Saxonicae (about 967-973), by book and chapter
sources.Ibrahim ibn Yaqub: a traveller from Tortosa, about 965; his account survives in al-Bakri's Kitab al-masalik wa'l-mamalik (1068)
sources.Thietmar: Thietmar of Merseburg, Chronicon (1012-1018), by book and chapter (Holtzmann's numbering)
sources.Adam of Bremen: Gesta Hammaburgensis ecclesiae pontificum (about 1075), by book and chapter
sources.Helmold: Helmold of Bosau, Chronica Slavorum (about 1170): late for our years, used only where marked
sources.DO I, DO II, DO III: the charters of Otto I, II and III in the MGH Diplomata, by number
sources.checked tonight: Wikipedia (de: Abodriten, Liutizen, Sachsenpfennig, Ralswiek; en: Lutici, Truso, Grobina, Wolin (town), Adalbert of Prague, Gottschalk (Obotrite prince), Pomerania during the Early Middle Ages), read 4 Oct 2026 for dates and names. Rimbert's chapter 30 could not be fetched from the Fordham sourcebook (the page was cut short); its numbers were confirmed from the Grobina page. Everything else is from the writer's knowledge of the sources and carries (?) where unsure.

needs: ports_793.json has no port for the Wilzi or the Pomeranians. Wolin (Jumne; about 53.84 N, 14.62 E; a trading place from about 800, great from about 950, burned 1043) is the one that matters most. Also: Menzlin on the Peene (about 750-900), Ralswiek on Rügen (about 780-1000), Starigard/Oldenburg (the Wagrians' fort, a see from about 968), Kołobrzeg (salt; a see in 1000), Gdańsk (a Polish fort from about 980; first named 997).
